title: Dottle and the Moonpetal Path
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks kept their watchtowers like fingers left out for stars. Terraces held villages the way palms hold water. Rivers talked to themselves all the way down. On one of those terraces, in a village that smelled of sunned stone and someone else’s baking, lived Dottle: a small goblin, quick, fingers like moonbeams that had learned useful work. His companion Nettle was a dragon the size of a pleased housecat. Her scales took the colours of oil on a wet road. When she was happy she purred like wind chimes that had decided not to hurry.

Dottle ran other people’s errands and did them well. He still felt, some mornings, like a polished bead dropped in a bucket of gravel.

Every day the work was ordinary. This morning it was not. He was to carry a single Moonpetal, cut with care from the highest cliffs, to the Elder Council. The bloom drank moonlight and gave it back as a shy lamp. It stood for clarity, for looking at a thing until it told the truth. Usually the Elder accepted it with a nod and a honey cake, and that was the whole ceremony.

Until the Elder, a gnome whose beard had ambitions of reaching the floor, cleared his throat as if announcing weather. “The Moonpetal. Most auspicious. You will remember the procession. Circle the ancient oak three times, for its wisdom. Present the bloom with the left hand; the right shall cup the elders’ contemplation. And Nettle will sing a traditional warding song to bless the journey.”

Dottle blinked. Nettle spoke in scale-shifts and chirps you could miss if you were busy being important. He pictured her on his shoulder, attempting an anthem. His mind, unhelpfully practical, began measuring the oak.

Because of that, he had only started a slightly crooked first circuit when a long shadow measured him first. Elara the elf arrived with a tape that seemed to have ideas about infinity. Her eyes treated the ground as a problem that could be solved if everyone stood still.

“Hold. Before any procession, the Moonpetal Path must be surveyed. We will not deviate by an acorn’s breadth.”

“The path to the Elder’s chamber,” Dottle said. “It has always been the path.”

“Ah, but is it?” Elara planted a flag that looked embarrassed among the roots. “Every pebble. Every incline. Accuracy is the bedrock of tradition. Without it we are simply lost.”

Because of that, a flower delivery became a career in maps. Elara drew until the parchment looked older than the mountain. She placed Dottle at angles and asked him to become geometry. She counted acorns. She counted the acorns again, in case the first count had been emotional. His useful mind, which liked solutions, rubbed raw against rules that multiplied when stared at. Nettle’s scales went a sympathetic grey. A neighbour passed, saw the flags, and decided the errand must be terribly important. Dottle, holding a flower that weighed less than a secret, did not correct them.

“It is a flower,” Dottle told her. “A luminous one. Still a flower.”

He knew who would hear that sentence without adding another flag. Further up the mountain, in huts that smelled of honey and wet earth, Dahlia Meadowsweet kept bees. She was an ogre whose hands could have been weapons and were, instead, careful.

Because of that, Dottle found her at the hive, moving as if the bees had invited her. “I have a Moonpetal,” he said, “and a procession that has grown hoops, and an elf who is measuring the air.”

Dahlia hummed. The sound went through the clearing like weather deciding to be kind. “Tradition is a river. It can water a field or cut a canyon. What do they actually want?”

Dottle looked at Nettle, who was watching a bee as if it were a small, flying relative. “They want to honour the bloom. They want to feel part of something large. Elara wants it to be correct.”

Dahlia gave him a scone still wearing honey. “Then show them that honour and correctness can meet. Your familiar is ingenious. Even a grand ritual is built of small true things.”

The scone did more than taste. It slowed him down. He went back. Elara was still drawing. The Elder was polishing a Sun-Kissed Thistle with a feather, which seemed to be another tradition nobody had explained.

Until finally Dottle spoke before the oak could be circled into nonsense. “Elara. You want the path measured. We will walk it together, step for step, and when the Moonpetal reaches the table it will have travelled exactly your distance.” To the Elder: “What if we do not dust it with pollen. Let its light fall on a dewdrop that has kept the morning. Clarity lives in small exact things as well as in processions.”

Elara’s tape paused in the air, a thin question. Dottle showed her the blade of grass. Nettle chirped and nudged a fallen Moonpetal leaf, silver at the edge, toward the drop. Light found water. For a breath the dewdrop became a private star. Wind moved in the oak. The parchment under Elara’s hand seemed, if you were inclined to poetry, to notice.

Dahlia had followed, quietly, as large people sometimes can. “And the song,” she said. “Perhaps Nettle offers it in the shimmer of her scales. A blessing you can see.”

Elara lowered the tape. She looked at the dewdrop, at Nettle’s pulse of colour, at the Elder, who had begun to beam as if someone had returned a borrowed idea improved. “A measured journey,” she said. “And a luminous dewdrop. That is precise. It is also, I admit, beautiful.”

The procession that followed had numbers in it, and therefore satisfied Elara, and light in it, and therefore satisfied the oak. They counted Dottle’s steps along the line she had already loved on paper. Nettle’s scales moved through colours the way evening moves through a valley. In the chamber Dottle set the Moonpetal beside the dewdrop. The two glows made a quiet that did not need a choir. Nobody clapped. The air did the smaller thing: it agreed.

Ever since then the errands still grew extra corners, because mountains enjoy a custom. Dottle no longer waited to be found in the gravel. He walked the counted path when counting mattered, and he left a little light on ordinary water when it did not, and Nettle, on his shoulder, kept the kind of silence that is also a song.
characters: Dottle (goblin with moonbeam-nimble fingers), Nettle (a housecat-sized dragon with oil-on-water scales), Dahlia Meadowsweet (an ogre beekeeper with a surprisingly soft voice)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
